newsitem.title: UK: U.S. stocks in London slip on weak dollar, IBM woes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks in London slip on weak dollar, IBM woes.

text.p: U.S. share prices were under pressure in London on Wednesday as investors worried that the dollar's slide in Asia overnight could herald a disposal of dollar-based assets by foreign investors, dealers said.

Standard & Poors 500 index futures took a dive in Asia, a move which some ascribed to a Wall Street Journal article suggesting that a slowdown in Japanese purchases of U.S. debt could depress U.S. markets.
Traders in Europe looked for a sharply lower opening on Wall Street, with sentiment also hit by rumours IBM may be on the verge of making a profit warning.
Trading in IBM shares came to a virtual halt in Europe after rumours circulated late morning of the possible profit warning, dealers here said.
"The market was already weak when the IBM rumour came flying around. It has really set the tone for the day," one senior dealer said. "The Dow is looking vulnerable."

Dealers here believe the Dow industrials average could lose 50 points at the 1430 GMT official open following the IBM profit rumours and as investors fret that foreign investors could abandon the U.S. stock market.

"Asset prices be they dollar, bonds or shares are overpriced in the U.S. There is a real worry in the market that the Japanese and other foreign investors may cut down on the buying of U.S. securities," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.
The dollar was steady in Europe after its one-pfenning fall overnight against the mark but remained under pressure against the yen.

The U.S. currency was hammered in Tokyo on Wednesday after news that Japan's October current account surplus with the U.S. had risen by 31.3 percent while its total surplus had fallen nearly 20 percent.

This data, coupled with news on Tuesday that the U.S. balance of payments was in the red by a record amount in the third quarter raised fears that foreign investment in U.S. securities may be overstretched.
U.S. current account figures on Tuesday also showed foreign investment in U.S. treasury bonds reached a record $42 billion in the third quarter while U.S. investment overseas was just $33 billion.
"The private sector of the market this year has been very wary of buying U.S. assets. The dollar has risen almost solely by concerted intervention by foreign central banks," Burke said.
"These central banks have record holdings of U.S. treasuries far in excess of the monetary base of the U.S. economy."

U.S. producer prices (PPI) will be the focus of market attention ahead of the Dow's opening. The November PPI is expected to rise by 0.3 percent month-on-month according to a Reuter poll of economists versus a 0.4 percent increase the previous month.
